topic: The Mathematics of Fair Sharing: Borsuk-Ulam and the Stolen Necklace
target_audience: Undergraduate students or advanced high school students with an interest in geometry and topology

sections.title: The Hook: The Thief's Dilemma
lecture_lines: Two thieves stole a ruby and emerald necklace.
They must share the beads perfectly in half.
What is the minimum number of cuts needed?
animations: Display a horizontal necklace with 6 rubies [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/ruby.svg] and 4 emeralds [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/emerald.svg] in a random sequence.
Show two rectangles 'Thief A' and 'Thief B' (#FFFFFF) and a central goal text: 'Goal: 3 Rubies, 2 Emeralds' (#FFFF00).
Animate a dashed vertical line (#FFFFFF) moving across the necklace to illustrate potential cuts.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Intermediate Value Theorem (1D Logic)
lecture_lines: Imagine an ant crawling up a hill.
To reach the top, it must pass the middle.
Continuous paths cannot skip intermediate values.
animations: Draw a brown curve (#8B4513) representing a hill from bottom-left to top-right.
Animate a blue circle (#0000FF) as the 'ant' moving along the curve from start to peak.
Add a yellow horizontal dashed line (#FFD700) at the midpoint, highlighting the intersection with the ant's path.

sections.title: The Borsuk-Ulam Theorem: Antipodal Points
lecture_lines: Imagine two opposite points on the Earth's surface.
These are called antipodal points on a sphere.
Borsuk-Ulam says opposite points share identical weather.
Temperature and pressure match at these locations.
A continuous mapping always finds this balanced pair.
animations: Draw a blue circle (#0000FF) representing Earth with 'T' (Temperature) and 'P' (Pressure) labels.
Draw a red diameter line (#FF0000) connecting two opposite points on the circle's perimeter.
Display 'T' and 'P' values at both ends of the diameter as it begins to rotate.
Animate the T and P values at the endpoints changing until both ends show identical values.
Flash the matching points in green (#00FF00) and label them 'Antipodal Balance'.

sections.title: Translating the Necklace to Geometry
lecture_lines: Wrap the necklace around a transparent ring.
A diameter represents a cut on both sides.
Rotating the diameter changes bead counts continuously.
animations: Transform the linear necklace from Section 1 into a circular ring, keeping the ruby and emerald positions.
Draw a white diameter line (#FFFFFF) through the center of the ring to represent cuts.
Rotate the diameter while updating text counters for rubies and emeralds for each side of the cut.

sections.title: Solving the Problem: The k-Color Solution
lecture_lines: For two bead types, two cuts are enough.
The theorem finds where bead differences are zero.
This logic extends to any number of varieties.
For k types, k cuts guarantee fair splits.
Topology proves a perfect solution always exists.
animations: Display the circular necklace with two rotating cut lines (represented by a diameter).
Show a 2D coordinate system with a blue vector tip representing the difference in ruby and emerald counts.
Animate the vector tip moving towards the origin (0, 0) as the diameter rotates.
Display 'k types = k cuts' in white text (#FFFFFF) as the vector hits the origin.
Highlight the final cut positions on the necklace with a gold glow (#FFD700).

sections.title: Conclusion and Visual Recap
lecture_lines: Topology ensures fairness through continuous geometric shapes.
Math proves solutions exist before we find them.
The thieves can now share their loot perfectly.
